title: Students are Novices, and That's Not a Bad Thing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to pushback on a prior article, Stuart defends treating all students as novices relative to the teacher, arguing this framing doesn't erase real differences among students but instead surfaces a deeper commonality that simplifies instructional decision-making. He distinguishes two domains of novice status: novice in the discipline being taught, and novice in the general discipline of learning itself. He's careful to frame novice status as relative and non-disrespectful, comparing it to being a novice at medicine or tax law, arguing that expertise gaps don't imply inferiority. Practically, he argues that teaching everyone as a novice removes the need for extensive ability grouping, since the same foundational instructional moves serve a wide range of actual skill levels. The piece links this idea to Woodenization, a concept from his book The Will to Learn.
points: Novice status is framed as relative to the teacher, not as a judgment of a student's worth or potential — just because a student is a novice doesn't mean they are less than the teacher.
Two distinct kinds of novice-hood matter: novice in the subject content itself, and novice in the general skill of learning, how to study, self-question, and direct one's own mind.

Practical payoff: treating all students as novices simplifies teaching by reducing the need for extensive ability grouping, since foundational scaffolding serves the full range of actual preparedness levels.
The piece explicitly connects the novice framing to Woodenization, Strategy 7 in The Will to Learn, tying this short reflection to a larger instructional system.
quotes: On one hand, no — thinking of our students as novices shouldn't negate the fact that each of them is very different from any other student I've ever taught. Each one has a different story, different likes and dislikes, different home lives, different relationships with all the other students in the room.
Anyone can point out how wide-ranging their rosters are; it takes an expert to focus on the deeper commonalities that all students share.
Just because a student is a novice doesn't mean they are less than me. It just means I have something that they don't; I've been to a place that I'm tasked with helping them move towards.
But look, I'm a novice in all sorts of settings. I'm a novice in medicine — that's why I go to a doctor. I'm a novice in tax law — that's why I go to an accountant.

But also, it's very practical because when you teach all of your students as if they are novices, your job becomes much simpler. I don't need to split the students into a bunch of ability groups — I can teach all of them what it takes to be the best possible student in my course.
